name: Mona Lisa
lede: Mona Lisa is a light, warm pink on web color lists; the name apparently borrows Leonardo's portrait, though the pink it suggests is the one the painting lost.

sections.title: A pink with a famous name
sections.body:
The swatch is a light, warm pink, #FF948E, which our library files in the pinks and places closest to [[salmon]] (5.6 units away) and, among near names, [[dusty-salmon]], in the family of [[light-salmon]] and plain [[pink]] [1]. The ISCC-NBS category nearest to it is strong pink, 5.4 units away [1].

Who named this pink, and when, is undocumented. Our library has the name from a single web color list and no dated printed source, and none of the 29 books gives it as a color [1]. The obvious guess is that it points to Leonardo's portrait, but no source we hold says so [1].

sections.title: The painting's lost pinks
sections.body:
Leonardo's portrait is dated c. 1502 by Ball and 1503-6 by Livingstone, so books disagree on the year [2][3]. By Ball's account Leonardo advised painting portraits in dull weather or at dusk, favored muted greens, blues and earth colors, and used sfumato, which lets colors drain into brown-black shadow away from the point of focus [2].

The pink of the name is probably not the color the portrait shows today. Gage notes that Leonardo's experimental techniques leave us unsure how his pictures looked, and that the rosy and pearly tints a sixteenth-century informant of Vasari described in the Mona Lisa have long since fled [4]. Ball calls the few surviving Leonardos sombre [2]. A pink swatch named for the painting is therefore closer to the color the portrait had than to the one it has [4].

sections.title: The smile that hides
sections.body:
Livingstone shows that the smile depends on where you look. Coarse image detail, which the edge of your vision favors, shows a clearer smile than fine detail does, so it seems to fade when your gaze lands on the mouth [3]. She suggests this explains the coy quality that Gombrich noticed [3]. The same low-resolution mixing is her explanation for the pearly look of Signac's gray [3].

Ball adds that the picture's fame now outruns its looks: crowds jostle to glimpse a dim, underlit portrait, and the painting has become a historical artefact more than a beauty [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of #FF948E covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 2 [6]. They are Louis Gustave Ricard's *[[painting:commons-Q17495200|Portrait de l'artiste]]* of 1853, at 12 per cent, and Correggio's *[[painting:nga-46167|Salvator Mundi]]* of 1515, at 9.6 per cent, where the pink sits in the lightest part of the picture [6]. Both are skin and cloth rather than sky or landscape. The caveat is the usual one: these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [6].
